newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: ITA depends on other countries joining - Brittan.
newsitem.headline: ITA depends on other countries joining - Brittan.

text.p: European Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan said on Thursday an agreement on scrapping tariffs on information technology products depended on enough countries joining the pact by March 15, 1997.
An Information Technology Agreement (ITA) depended upon agreement from countries representing about 90 percent of the trade in the sector, Brittan told a news conference.

"Clearly, both Europe and the United States made it clear that this is not a bilateral agreement. It's meant to be agreement covering the countries in the world most involved in this whole area of activity," he said.

"Participants will implement the actions foreseen in the declaration providing the participants representing approximately 90 percent of world trade in information technology products have by then, that is by March 15, 1997, notified their acceptance," he said, quoting from the draft declaration agreed by the United States and European Council.
But Brittan said the 90 percent was not "a rigid barrier".
Brittan also said there is "a provision for accelerating the staging provisions which at the moment provide for the elimination of tariffs by the year 2000."

Therefore, he said, "there is also a provision which says that the implementation of the agreement is conditional upon participants being satisfied with the outcome of the further staging talks that will take place about accelerating of the provisions."
A European Union spokesman said earlier on Thursday the council had earlier endorsed an agreement with the United States on a global information technology trade pact.
The council met after an early morning briefing between Acting U.S. trade representative Charlene Barshefsky and European Trade Commissioner Leon Brittan.
Barshefksy had earlier expressed doubts about European commitment to the ITA accord and the European's earlier

The European Council endorsement clears a major obstacle for a information technology accord that would eliminate tariffs on a wide range of computer products at this week's World Trade Organisation (WTO) ministerial meeting.
A U.S. official told reporters a total of 20 countries had committed themselves to the deal. These were the 15 European Union nations, the U.S., Canada, Japan, plus Hong Kong and Singapore.
"It is very encouraging. We are heading towards a real critical mass, but we do need some more Asians coming on board," said the official, who declined to be identified.
The U.S. is known to be particularly anxious to get Thailand and Malaysia into the deal.
A Singapore official said his country accounted for about four percent of world trade in IT.

The U.S. official said among the items the U.S. wanted in the deal and had been included were digital still cameras, digital copiers, set-top TV boxes, graphic display tubes and interactive audio-visual products. Fibre optic cable was also included, but optic fibre strands are excluded. Basic, non-digital, office copiers are excluded.
"The critical step now is to get the Asians fully on board," the official said. "The objective is to get maximum product coverage by the year 2000. We have to get 90 percent."
"We are now working with all our trading partners and we need to get a step forward from the U.S. and the European Union and the rest of the Quad," he added.
About another 15 countries outside of the Quad are involved in the talks.
